KEY MESSAGE 1...Widespread cloud coverage over eastern NY and 
western New England continues into this afternoon as we remain 
north of a sfc warm front positioned in far southeastern 
NY/northern NJ. However, the mid-level warm front has started to
advance northeastward and dew points are creeping further into
the upper 60s to low 70s. With the latest visible satellite
showing some thinning to the cloud coverage, the increased
insolation combined with an increasingly moist environment is
contributing to increased instability. The latest SPC mesoscale
analysis shows meager ML CAPE values around 500 - 1000 J/kg 
mainly south and west of the Hudson River with instability
quickly trending downwards into the Capital District and north 
and east. PWATs are quite high today well over 1.5" as the 
latest ALPW satellite channels show a moisture plume from the 
Southeast U.S and western Atlantic nosing northward. Forecast 
soundings also show that this highly moist environment will also
feature high freezing level heights 12-13 kft and high EL 
heights supporting a tall- skinny CAPE sounding. With effective 
shear also decent at 25 - 35kts, today is a classic environment 
that favors heavy downpours and this continues to be the primary
hazard for today. We considered a flood watch for the mid- 
Hudson Valley where WPC maintains its slight risk in the Day 1 
Excessive Rainfall Outlook; however, decided to hold off given 
this area missed out on the heavy rain this morning and it 
remained mainly to the south. While the latest 3-hrly 
precipitation PMM from the HREF still shows a 10 to localized 
30% chance for 3" of rain in three hours in the mid-Hudson 
Valley and eastern Catskills late this afternoon into this 
evening, the latest 3-hr FFG remain quite high at 2.5 - 3.5". 
Thus, even if these rainfall rates are realized, rainfall 
amounts may just reach FFG. If heavy rain repeatedly impacts a 
given area, it will likely become vulnerable to localized 
flooding including even isolated to scattered flash flooding but
confidence is too low to warrant a flood watch. 

Besides heavy rain resulting in localized flooding, severe
thunderstorms resulting in damaging winds is a secondary hazard
for today. As was mentioned, forecast sounding overall meager 
instability with the highest values south/east of the Capital 
District. However, favorable effective shear 30 - 40kts combined
with sufficient instability can support bowing segments and 
QLCS type structures as the warm front lifts northward. 
Damaging winds are the primary hazard from any severe storms 
but southeast winds in the low-levels quickly veering to the 
west-southwest aloft have led to curved hodographs and enhanced 
effective helicity values along the warm front to 100-200m2/s2. 
This means isolated tornadoes are not ruled out, especially 
given low LCLs values. Thus, we have collaborated with SPC and 
neighboring WFOs to issue a Tornado Watch through 9PM this 
evening for the Mohawk Valley, western Adirondacks, northern and
eastern Catskills, mid-Hudson Valley and NW CT. Very high EL 
heights also makes this a favorable environment for frequent 
lightning. Latest CAMs have struggled capturing latest radar 
trends but as convection from the Southern Tier and southeast NY
tracks north and east later this afternoon, it will run into a 
less favorable environment and weaken. Thus, the latest Tornado
Watch does not extend into the Capital District or areas north 
and east. Any initial strong to severe storms should weaken 
late this afternoon as the environments gets worked over and 
transition to more of a hydro concern. Some showers will still 
be around tonight as the warm front finally pushes north and 
east but will diminish in coverage. Otherwise, it will remain 
very muggy.

The warm sector shifts eastward tomorrow as the main cold front
and trough axis swings into the Northeast. Given the early 
arrival of the cold front pushing into the eastern NY by 15 - 18
UTC, the highest chance for the warm sector to have enough time
to destabilize before the strongest forcing arrives look to be 
in areas mainly east of the Hudson River, especially in western 
New England. The latest Day 2 SPC Outlook continues to place a 
marginal (level 1 of 5) risk for severe weather in southern 
Berkshire and Litchfield Counties where there is a favorable 
overlap of 500-1000J/kg of SB CAPE and 40-45kts of deep layer 
shear. Latest CAMs shows an initial line of showers developing
along the incoming cold front late morning that grows upscale 
into line segments and storm clusters as it enters western New 
England and the more unstable environment mainly after 17-18 
UTC. Damaging winds will also again be the main hazard through 
late afternoon before the front finally pushes eastward into 
New England. Otherwise, humidity will trend downwards behind 
the cold front from west to east through the day with clearing 
skies.
